x.ASV: Maschil of Asaph. O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? Why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?
x.Darby: An instruction: of Asaph. Why, OGod, hast thou cast off for ever? [why] doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?
x.KJV: Maschil of Asaph. O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?
x.YLT: An Instruction of Asaph. Why, O God, hast Thou cast off for ever? Thine anger smoketh against the flock of Thy pasture.

nt: The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language.
לָ⁠מָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים זָנַ֣חְתָּ לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח יֶעְשַׁ֥ן אַ֝פְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠צֹ֣אן מַרְעִיתֶֽ⁠ךָ

Asaph is using the question form to express his anguish at God’s anger toward his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God, you have rejected us forever! Your nose should not smoke against the flock of your pasture.]

Asaph is using **does your nose smoke** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why are you angry]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were **the flock** of a shepherd, and of God as if he were a shepherd who cares for them in **your pasture**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against the people you care for]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **flock** that is associated with a **pasture**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [against the flock that you pasture]

x.ASV: Remember thy congregation, which thou hast gotten of old, Which thou hast redeemed to be the tribe of thine inheritance; And mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt.
x.Darby: Remember thine assembly, which thou hast purchased of old, which thou hast redeemed [to be] the portion of thine inheritance, this mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt.
x.KJV: Remember thy congregation, which thou hast purchased of old; the rod of thine inheritance, which thou hast redeemed; this mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt.
x.YLT: Remember Thy company. Thou didst purchase of old, Thou didst redeem the rod of Thy inheritance, This mount Zion--Thou didst dwell in it.

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. See the Introduction to this Psalm for more information on how to translate the imperative here and throughout this Psalm. Alternate translation: [Please remember your congregation]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean that the tribe itself is what God inherited. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tribe that is your inheritance]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the tribe that you inherited] or [the people whom you have made your own]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that a sentence in many languages would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if this would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [remember this Mount Zion on which you have dwelt]

x.ASV: Lift up thy feet unto the perpetual ruins, All the evil that the enemy hath done in the sanctuary.
x.Darby: Lift up thy steps unto the perpetual desolations: everything in the sanctuary hath the enemy destroyed.
x.KJV: Lift up thy feet unto the perpetual desolations; even all that the enemy hath done wickedly in the sanctuary.
x.YLT: Lift up Thy steps to the perpetual desolations, Everything the enemy did wickedly in the sanctuary.

nt: The psalmist speaks of God as if he were a person with **feet** which he could **Lift up** and come and see the ruined temple in Jerusalem. The phrase **Lift up your feet** is probably also indicating that the psalmist wants God to not only take notice but also to take notice quickly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come and see the perpetual ruins] or [Please do not delay any longer. Please pay attention to these perpetual ruins]

Here and other places in this psalm, **the holy place** refers to the Temple in Jerusalem that had been destroyed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly as modeled by the UST.

x.ASV: Thine adversaries have roared in the midst of thine assembly; They have set up their ensigns for signs.
x.Darby: Thine adversaries roar in the midst of thy place of assembly; they set up their signs [for] signs.
x.KJV: Thine enemies roar in the midst of thy congregations; they set up their ensigns for signs.
x.YLT: Roared have thine adversaries, In the midst of Thy meeting-places, They have set their ensigns as ensigns.

nt: Here Asaph is speaking of the **adversaries** as if they were wild animals that **roared**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your adversaries shouted loudly]

Setting up **signs** was a symbolic action by which the conquerors signified their victory over those conquered. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The phrase **they have set up their signs as signs** could mean: (1) that God’s adversaries had set up their military banners as signs in the Temple. Alternate translation: [they have set up their banners as signs] or [they have set up their banners as a sign of their conquest] or (2) that God’s adversaries had set up items of worship and symbols related to their false religion. Alternate translation: [they have set up symbols and items for their pagan worship] or [they have set up idolatrous symbols and items of false worship]

x.ASV: They seemed as men that lifted up Axes upon a thicket of trees.
x.Darby: [A man] was known as he could lift up axes in the thicket of trees;
x.KJV: A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees.
x.YLT: He is known as one bringing in on high Against a thicket of wood--axes.

nt: The expression **It was known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They appeared]

The point of this comparison is that just as a woodsman swings **axes** to cut down trees **in a thicket**, so the enemies swung their weapons to destroy the carvings of the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a woodsman chopping down trees in a forest]

x.ASV: And now all the carved work thereof They break down with hatchet and hammers.
x.Darby: And now they break down its carved work altogether, with hatchets and hammers.
x.KJV: But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers.
x.YLT: And now, its carvings together With axe and hatchet they break down,

nt: Here the words **And now** mark a shift from describing what the enemies did in the past to what they are doing in the present. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Now]
The pronoun **its** refers to the holy place. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the carvings of the holy place]

x.ASV: They have set thy sanctuary on fire; They have profaned the dwelling-place of thy name by casting it to the ground.
x.Darby: They have set on fire thy sanctuary, they have profaned the habitation of thy name to the ground.
x.KJV: They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
x.YLT: They have sent into fire Thy sanctuary, to the earth they polluted the tabernacle of Thy name,

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on translating parallelisms, see the Introduction to this Psalm. Alternate translation: [They completely burned down and desecrated the place where you dwell]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemies sent]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the place called by your name by bringing it] or [the dwelling where you are present by bringing it]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **dwelling** that is characterized by God’s **name**, that is, by his presence. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the dwelling place dedicated to you by burning it]

x.ASV: They said in their heart, Let us make havoc of them altogether: They have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.
x.Darby: They said in their heart, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up allGod's places of assembly in the land.
x.KJV: They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.
x.YLT: They said in their hearts, `Let us oppress them together,' They did burn all the meeting-places of God in the land.

nt: The phrase **They said in their heart** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [They thought to themselves]
Both occurrences of the pronoun **They** refer to the enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemies said in their heart]

Asaph is using **in their heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the enemies thought this to themselves. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [within themselves]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the places that are dedicated to **God** for worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the places where people gather to worship God]

x.ASV: We see not our signs: There is no more any prophet; Neither is there among us any that knoweth how long.
x.Darby: We see not our signs; there is no more any prophet, neither is there among us any that knoweth how long.
x.KJV: We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long.
x.YLT: Our ensigns we have not seen, There is no more a prophet, Nor with us is one knowing how long.

nt: Here the phrase **our signs** could refer to: (1) signs that God’s prophets gave. Alternate translation: [We do not see any prophetic signs for us] or [We do not see any signs given to us from a prophet] or (2) the military banners and symbols used by the Israelite army which represented their army. Alternate translation: [We no longer see any of our military banners] or (3) the Jewish festivals and religious observances which were the outward signs of their religion. Alternate translation: [We no longer see any signs of our religion] or [All our sacred observances are gone] or [All our sacred symbols are gone]

x.ASV: How long, O God, shall the adversary reproach? Shall the enemy blaspheme thy name for ever?
x.Darby: How long, OGod, shall the adversary reproach? Shall the enemy contemn thy name for ever?
x.KJV: O God, how long shall the adversary reproach? shall the enemy blaspheme thy name for ever?
x.YLT: Till when, O God, doth an adversary reproach? Doth an enemy despise thy name for ever?

nt: עַד־מָתַ֣י אֱ֭לֹהִים יְחָ֣רֶף צָ֑ר יְנָ֘אֵ֤ץ אוֹיֵ֖ב שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לָ⁠נֶֽצַח

Asaph is using the question form to express his impatient plea for God to intervene. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [God, the adversary has reproached you long enough! The enemy should not despise your name forever.]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

x.ASV: Why drawest thou back thy hand, even thy right hand? Pluck it out of thy bosom and consume them.
x.Darby: Why withdrawest thou thy hand, and thy right hand? [pluck it] out of thy bosom: consume [them].
x.KJV: Why withdrawest thou thy hand, even thy right hand? pluck it out of thy bosom.
x.YLT: Why dost Thou turn back Thy hand, Even Thy right hand? From the midst of Thy bosom remove it.

nt: Asaph is using the question form to protest God’s inaction. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not hold back your hand, even your right hand!]

Asaph is using **hold back your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is withholding his action and not intervening. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do you refrain from acting with your great power]

Here, **your hand, even your right hand** represents God’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your power, even your great strength]

Here, **your bosom** represents concealment and inaction, as though God were keeping his hand tucked inside his robe instead of stretching it out to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your hiding place]

x.ASV: Yet God is my King of old, Working salvation in the midst of the earth.
x.Darby: ButGod is my king of old, accomplishing deliverances in the midst of the earth.
x.KJV: For God is my King of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.
x.YLT: And God is my king of old, Working salvation in the midst of the earth.

nt: Asaph uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the despair he has expressed about the destruction of the temple and his confidence in God as king. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yet God is my king]
Asaph uses the pronoun **my** instead of “our” to express a personal declaration of trust. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is my king whom I trust]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [mighty things to save his people]

x.ASV: Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: Thou brakest the heads of the sea-monsters in the waters.
x.Darby: Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength; thou didst break the heads of the monsters on the waters:
x.KJV: Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters.
x.YLT: Thou hast broken by Thy strength a sea- monster, Thou hast shivered Heads of dragons by the waters,

nt: Asaph is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb translated as **you divided** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was God himself who performed this mighty act. If it would be natural in your language to use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation, or you could express this emphasis in a different way. See how you as a team decide to translate this phrase and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [It was you who divided]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are strong]

Here Asaph is speaking of the forces of chaos as if they were **sea monsters** whose **heads** God crushed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the powers of the chaotic waters]

x.ASV: Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces; Thou gavest him to be food to the people inhabiting the wilderness.
x.Darby: Thou didst break in pieces the heads of leviathan, thou gavest him to be meat to those that people the desert.
x.KJV: Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces, and gavest him to be meat to the people inhabiting the wilderness.
x.YLT: Thou hast broken the heads of leviathan, Thou makest him food, For the people of the dry places.

nt: Here Asaph is speaking of the forces of chaos as if they were a great sea creature called **Leviathan**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the great chaos creature]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s defeat of Leviathan as if God had given **him as food** to people, meaning that God completely destroyed this power. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you left his remains for the people]

x.ASV: Thou didst cleave fountain and flood: Thou driedst up mighty rivers.
x.Darby: Thou didst cleave fountain and torrent, thou driedst up ever-flowing rivers.
x.KJV: Thou didst cleave the fountain and the flood: thou driedst up mighty rivers.
x.YLT: Thou hast cleaved a fountain and a stream, Thou hast dried up perennial flowings.

nt: Here, **split open spring and wadi** refers to Yahweh breaking open the ground and causing springs and streams to flow. Alternate translation: [you caused springs and streams to flow out of the ground]

x.ASV: The day is thine, the night also is thine: Thou hast prepared the light and the sun.
x.Darby: The day is thine, the night also is thine; thou hast prepared the moon and the sun:
x.KJV: The day is thine, the night also is thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun.
x.YLT: Thine is the day, also Thine is the night, Thou hast prepared a light giver--the sun.

nt: Asaph is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **the day** and **the night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All hours of the day and night are also]

Here the word **also** connects two parallel statements, emphasizing that both the day and the night belong to God. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [even]

Asaph is referring to all celestial light by naming two components, **the light and the sun**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every source of light in the sky]

x.ASV: Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: Thou hast made summer and winter.
x.Darby: Thou hast set all the borders of the earth; summer and winter — thou didst form them.
x.KJV: Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter.
x.YLT: Thou hast set up all the borders of earth, Summer and winter Thou hast formed them.

nt: Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the boundaries that mark the extent of **the earth**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the boundaries that define the earth]

Asaph is referring to all the seasons of the year by naming two extremes, **summer and winter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the seasons of the year]

x.ASV: Remember this, that the enemy hath reproached, O Jehovah, And that a foolish people hath blasphemed thy name.
x.Darby: Remember this, that an enemy hath reproached Jehovah, and a foolish people have contemned thy name.
x.KJV: Remember this, that the enemy hath reproached, O Lord, and that the foolish people have blasphemed thy name.
x.YLT: Remember this--an enemy reproached Jehovah, And a foolish people have despised Thy name.

nt: Here the words **Remember this** mark a shift from praising God’s mighty acts back to petitioning him for help. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Consider this]

Even though Asaph is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **Yahweh** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [the enemy has reproached you, Yahweh]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [has despised your reputation]

x.ASV: Oh deliver not the soul of thy turtle-dove unto the wild beast: Forget not the life of thy poor for ever.
x.Darby: Give not up the soul of thy turtle-dove unto the wild beast; forget not the troop of thine afflicted for ever.
x.KJV: O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked: forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever.
x.YLT: Give not up to a company, The soul of Thy turtle-dove, The company of Thy poor ones forget not for ever.

nt: Asaph is using the possessive form to describe the **life** that belongs to the people he calls a **dove**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the lives of your people whom you cherish]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were a vulnerable **dove**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your defenseless people]

Here Asaph is speaking of the enemy nation as if it were a wild **beast** that would devour its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the cruel enemy]

Asaph is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your poor people]

x.ASV: Have respect unto the covenant; For the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of violence.
x.Darby: Have respect unto the covenant; for the dark places of the earth are full of the dwellings of violence.
x.KJV: Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty.
x.YLT: Look attentively to the covenant, For the dark places of earth, Have been full of habitations of violence.

nt: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because violent places fill the dark places of the land]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe **pastures** that are characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent places]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent deeds]

Here Asaph is speaking of places of oppression and danger as if they were **dark places**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the dangerous places of the land]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the places in **the land** that are dark, that is, dangerous. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the dark places that are in the land]

x.ASV: Oh let not the oppressed return ashamed: Let the poor and needy praise thy name.
x.Darby: Oh let not the oppressed one return ashamed; let the afflicted and needy praise thy name.
x.KJV: O let not the oppressed return ashamed: let the poor and needy praise thy name.
x.YLT: Let not the oppressed turn back ashamed, Let the poor and needy praise Thy name,

nt: Asaph is using the adjective **weak** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the weak person]

The expression **ashamed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [feeling shame]

Asaph is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who are poor and needy]

x.ASV: Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: Remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee all the day.
x.Darby: Rise up, OGod, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee all the day;
x.KJV: Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily.
x.YLT: Arise, O God, plead Thy plea, Remember Thy reproach from a fool all the day.

nt: Here the words **Arise, God** mark a shift to a final urgent appeal for God to act. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Take action, God]

Here Asaph is speaking of God as if he were a litigant who would **plead** a legal **case** in court. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Contend for yourself]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the case that is brought against God, that is, the insults directed at him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the case against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the fool reproaches you]
Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the reproach that comes from **the fool**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the way the fool reproaches you]

x.ASV: Forget not the voice of thine adversaries: The tumult of those that rise up against thee ascendeth continually.
x.Darby: Forget not the voice of thine adversaries: the tumult of those that rise up against thee ascendeth continually.
x.KJV: Forget not the voice of thine enemies: the tumult of those that rise up against thee increaseth continually.
x.YLT: Forget not the voice of Thine adversaries, The noise of Thy withstanders is going up continually!

nt: Here, **the voice of your adversaries** represents what the adversaries are saying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the words of your adversaries]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the voice that comes from **your adversaries**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [what your adversaries are saying]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the uproar that comes from **the ones rising against** God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the noise that your opponents make]
